Review Body:
Review of The Body Keeps the Score by Bessel van der Kolk

I came to this book at precisely the right moment in my life, thanks to the recommendation of my naturopathic doctor, Taggy Bensaid. At the time, I was about six months into therapy for my own PTSD and just beginning to explore deeper healing approaches. This book became a guidepost, illuminating the intersections of trauma, healing, and the holistic therapies I was already embracing, like music, massage, and yoga.

One of the most powerful lessons I took from this book is the understanding that many behaviors—especially in children—aren’t willful defiance or laziness, but expressions of unprocessed trauma. It reinforced my belief that society, as a whole, has a responsibility to address the growing epidemic of trauma, not just by treating individuals but by creating environments that foster healing and growth.

This resonated deeply with me as both a teacher and a choir member. It explained why I’ve struggled with breathing properly in choir and gave me tools to approach teaching with more compassion—not as a disciplinarian, but as someone committed to understanding what’s happening in a child’s world before taking action.

On a personal level, this book affirmed my vision for strengthening connections within my extended family. Too often, I’ve encountered resistance in the form of phrases like, “People have to take care of their own families,” or “You can’t make people do what they don’t want to do.” This book helped me see those responses in a new light, rooted in their own unprocessed experiences, and gave me renewed determination to move beyond that negativity.

The Body Keeps the Score isn’t just a book—it’s a lifeline for anyone seeking to understand trauma and chart a path toward healing. It’s accessible, insightful, and profoundly validating, and I’m grateful to have encountered it at such a pivotal time in my life.

Review Body:
"We now know that there is another possible response to threat, which our scans aren't capable of measuring. Some people simply go into denial: Their bodies register the threat, but their conscious minds go on as if nothing has happened. However, even though the mind may learn to ignore the messages from the emotional brain, the alarm signals don't stop. The emotional brain keeps working, and stress hormones keep sending signals to the muscles to tense for action or immobilize in collapse. The physical effects on the organs go on unabated until they demand notice when they are expressed as illness. Medications, drugs, and alcohol can also temporarily dull or obliterate unbearable sensations and feelings. But the body continues to keep the score."

I’ve dedicated January 2025 to reading books that have been languishing on my TBR list. The Body Keeps the Score is the first of four that I’ve chosen. I became interested in reading this after it was recommend by a podcaster I regularly listen to. I started and stopped it a couple of times in 2024. I wasn’t fully prepared for how dense it is.

The book begins with a history of the development of the modern medical approach to mental suffering and includes many examples from the author's own education and practice. There are a lot of scientific details and uncomfortable accounts of child abuse, sexual assaults, and wartime atrocities.

Things I liked:

The chapter on the body-brain connections, particularly the description of fight, flight, or freeze and the reasons behind the physical manifestations we experience during these states.

The part that discusses the paths to recovery. It was interesting to read about various treatment modalities.

Things I didn't like:

This is a long book and I kind of got lost in all the words. I feel like the word count could have been cut in half and it would have been a much more understandable read.

The author speaks of repressed memories as settled fact, but they have not been supported by research and are not universally accepted as true.

The details of various traumas, particularly child sexual abuse, seemed unnecessary and could be triggering for some individuals. I feel like this was an unwise inclusion in a book geared to people who have experienced trauma.

There is no discussion of the resiliency of humans. If you were to believe this book, everyone who has experienced trauma would be unable to function without professional help, but many do recover on their own and go on to live healthy, well adjusted lives.

I am glad I read this book to have an idea of what everyone is talking about and it did give me some things to think about, but I am surprised that it is so popular with such high reviews. It was a slog for me and I'm glad to be done reading it.
